title: Claypot Rice
subtitle: Jasmine rice cooked with lap cheong, chicken, and dark soy in a clay pot
excerpt: Cooking rice in a clay pot over a flame creates a crispy scorched crust at the bottom -- the most prized part -- while the top layer steams perfectly tender. Lap cheong and marinated chicken sit on top and cook through on the steam. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Bo zai fan (claypot rice) is a winter speciality of Cantonese cooking, sold from street stalls in Hong Kong and Guangzhou throughout the cooler months. The technique of cooking rice in an unglazed clay pot over charcoal originated in rural Guangdong and is documented in Cantonese food histories as far back as the Qing dynasty. The clay pot's porous walls regulate heat unevenly, creating the characteristic crust at the base that distinguishes claypot rice from rice cooker rice.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the chicken the night before. The rice must be cooked and eaten fresh -- it does not hold well.

content.text: This serves 4 and takes about 55 minutes from start to table. The technique relies on a
clay pot
-- its porous, unglazed walls absorb and distribute heat in a way that coaxes a golden crust (fan jiu) from the bottom layer of
jasmine rice
while the top steams soft. A heavy-based saucepan works as a substitute but will not develop the same crust.

The most important step is listening: when the sound from the pot changes from a simmer to a light crackling, the crust is forming. That is the moment to drizzle in the soy sauce around the rim and turn off the heat. Leave the lid on for another 5 minutes so the residual heat finishes the toppings without drying out the rice.
What you need

items.prepNote: boneless, skinless, cut into 3 cm pieces

content.text: Method
Combine the chicken marinade ingredients and toss with the chicken pieces. Leave to marinate for at least 15 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Lightly oil the inside of the clay pot with a few drops of vegetable oil. Add the rinsed jasmine rice and pour over the 400 ml of water. The water should sit about 2 cm above the surface of the rice.

Place the clay pot over medium heat without a lid. Bring the water to the boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Once the surface of the rice begins to show steam vents (small craters forming in the surface), lay the marinated chicken pieces evenly over the top. Arrange the
lap cheong
slices between the chicken.
Put the lid on and cook over the lowest possible heat for 15 minutes. The steam trapped inside will cook the chicken and sausage through while the base of the rice develops a crust.
Listen for the sound to shift from simmering to a quiet crackling. This signals that the water has evaporated and the crust is forming. At this point, lift the lid slightly and pour the finishing
dark soy sauce
around the inner rim of the pot so it trickles down the sides. Replace the lid.

Turn off the heat and leave the pot to rest, lid on, for 5 minutes. Scatter over the sliced spring onions, then bring the entire pot to the table. Scrape the crust from the bottom as you serve -- it should come away in golden shards.

items.symptom: Rice is undercooked in the centre
items.cause: Heat was too low, or the lid was lifted too early
items.fix: Replace the lid and cook for a further 5 minutes on low. Avoid lifting the lid until the crackling stage.

items.symptom: The crust has burnt rather than crisped
items.cause: Heat was too high at the final stage
items.fix: The crackling sound should be gentle, not fierce. If it sounds aggressive, turn the heat off immediately. The residual heat in the clay pot will finish the crust.

items.cause: Pieces were too thick or were placed on top too late
items.fix: Cut chicken into pieces no thicker than 2 cm. If unsure, slice a piece to check before serving -- return to the pot with the lid on for an extra 3 minutes if needed.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Bo zai fan is intimately tied to Hong Kong winter street culture. Stalls in Sham Shui Po and Wan Chai set up rows of gas burners and clay pots in the cooler months, and queues form for bowls where the scorched rice crust (fan jiu) is considered the cook's signature. The dish is inherently a single-portion, single-pot meal -- the clay pot comes to the table and diners eat directly from it with chopsticks, mixing the sweet lap cheong fat and dark soy through the white rice as they go.
